newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Thai central banker moves out, IMF moves in.
newsitem.headline: Thai central banker moves out, IMF moves in.

text.p: Thailand's central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond has resigned in the week when the International Monetary Fund (IMF) goes to Bangkok to advise the government on ways to help revive the country's ailing economy.
Analysts said on Tuesday they suspected the two events may not be entirely unrelated, given the possibility the IMF advice may run contrary to policies put in place by the central bank.

Rerngchai was the target of those critical of his handling of problems in the finance sector and by a corporate sector suffering agonies due to the central bank's insistence that interest rates be kept high to defend the baht.
"It may just be a coincidence of course, but Rerngchai has gone just as the IMF came to town," said one analyst who declined to be named.
"The IMF are going to be pretty tough if lines of credit are going to be arranged and that could well mean flying in the face of the central bank."
The Thai authorities have changed their tune over the credit issue. At first they said they were seeking IMF assistance but there was no question of loans.
Later, Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya said the need for standby credit lines would be studied and it was then the markets really started to take heart.
The baht and the Thai stock market were also boosted by an offer from Japan's Ministry of Finance to consider making loans to Thailand should they be requested.
The onshore baht rallied to within a whisker of 30 per U.S. dollar on a surge of optimism after the credit line news and the notoriously volatile stock market rallied over two percent.
"The sort of external credibility that Thailand needs can only be got through an IMF credit line," said one analyst at a European investment bank in Singapore.
Estimates of how much cash help Thailand needs varies widely with some analysts looking for US$3-5 billion while others see more like US$10-20 billion.
"I don't think the amount is the key issue," the European bank analyst said. "It's the signal it sends to the markets that is important."
She said that in the Mexico crisis, after the IMF stepped in, around US$44 billion of non-IMF loans were mobilised.
"It's what I call the policy collateral of the switch of the economic course which is important. It means other credit lines can, and will, be arranged."

So good news for the markets in general, but what does it mean for the two-tier currency system in place since Thailand imposed capital controls to try and defend the baht, a move which starved offshore speculative players of liquidity.
Under the controls, the central bank made it considerably harder for offshore speculators to borrow baht to buy dollars than for domestic players.

"If they want the IMF to help, I'm sure the IMF will require them to get rid of capital controls and dismantle the two-tier system," said Philip Wee Sung Seng, regional treasury economist at Standard Chartered. "They need the capital flows very badly."
Up to now the market has suspected the Thai authorities would wait until the speculative three month forward positions, which were put on at the start of the baht crisis, had matured.
This would be around the middle of August, but it could come sooner with August 5 seen as a date which is growing in importance.
Thailand has said it will publish the economic rescue package before August 5 and the market is betting it will be published that day. There may also be some other surprises.
"I think the two-tier system will come to an end sooner than people expect. You never know everything may be announced on August 5," Standard Chartered's Philip Wee said.
